title: As crypto and prediction markets expand, their regulator shrinks
description: President Donald Trump shakes hands with
body:
President Donald Trump shakes hands with Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) Chairman Michael Selig during a meeting with technology leaders in the Roosevelt Room of the White House, Wednesday, Aug. 19, 2026, in Washington.
                
                    Jacquelyn Martin/Associated Press
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jacquelyn Martin/Associated Press
    

   
   Trump-era staff reductions have significantly hampered enforcement at the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and its ability to regulate burgeoning new prediction and cryptocurrency markets, where hundreds of billions are traded each week.   By the end of 2025, the CFTC had 21% fewer staff on its payroll when compared to the previous 10-year average, according to U.S. Office of Personnel Management data. Between January 2024 and January 2025 alone, staffing dropped 22%. And the number of CFTC enforcement actions dropped even further. The agency made nearly 80% fewer enforcement actions in 2025 when compared to the annual average for the previous decade, according to the agency's annual reports.   
   The CFTC started hemorrhaging staff soon after President Trump won the 2024 election. This was not a coincidence, according to Jeff Le Riche, who worked as a CFTC enforcement lawyer between 2005 and 2025.   "The Trump administration had run partially on a platform that it would be friendlier to the crypto industry," Le Riche said.   Leading up to the 2024 election, the CFTC under the Biden administration had leveled enforcement cases against cryptocurrency companies such as Gemini, Mirror Trading, Voyager, Celsius and FTX for fraud. It did the same against the crypto prediction market Polymarket.   After President Trump's inauguration, "in order to show results to that industry, some people were punished for bringing those cases," Le Riche continued. "The end result was that a lot of the people that worked on those cases either left or were forced out."   
   In a statement to NPR, the CFTC did not address that claim directly, but praised the work of current agency head Michael Selig.   "The CFTC remains committed to promoting integrity and responsible innovation in U.S. derivatives markets, and Chairman Selig is grateful to the dedicated staff who continue to support this mission each day," CFTC spokesman Zach Fulton wrote in part.   
   To Le Riche, the 21% drop in employees and the nearly 80% decline in enforcement action go hand in hand.   "It castrated the enforcement team," Le Riche said. "Many of the people who were targeted were high-performing attorneys who had brought some of the most consequential and complicated cases over the past few years."   Joe Konizeski, who worked as a CFTC enforcement lawyer for 26 years, was one of the dozens forced out in 2025.   
   "The acting chair [Caroline Pham] said, 'We're closing all our crypto [cases],'" Konizeski said. "And so, of course, everybody who had a crypto scam had to close it and any matter that was even marginally related to crypto ended up getting closed."   Pham left the CFTC in December of 2025 and is now the chief legal and administrative officer at MoonPay, a cryptocurrency company. She did not respond to NPR's request for comment about whether she gave preferential treatment to the crypto industry.   Since Trump took office, the CFTC has rolled back its enforcement actions against crypto firms Gemini, Celsius, and FTX. But crypto cases weren't the only ones impacted. Konizeski said decreased staffing caused the CFTC to dismiss others such as a foreign exchange fraud case against WorldWideMarkets Inc. The company was accused of defrauding millions from users.   
   Before the explosion of the crypto and prediction markets, the CFTC largely focused on more traditional derivative markets — such as grain and stock futures contracts.   "Fewer cops on the beat… creates a real incentive to start engaging in fraudulent and deceitful behavior," Konizeski said. "Enforcement is down and that means that there's going to be more fraud."   
   For Konizeski, chief examples of this are prediction market advertisements that target young men. He accused Polymarket and Kalshi of "using fraudulent means" to entice young men to its platforms.   "CFTC knows this and allows it to continue," Konizeski said.   Neither Polymarket nor Kalshi responded to NPR's requests for comment about whether their advertising targeted young men.   A former CFTC lawyer, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of professional repercussions, said they left the agency voluntarily soon after Trump took office and Pham curbed enforcement.   "Enforcement was particularly closed in crypto and prediction market cases," this former CFTC staffer said. "A lot of people left because, once Pham took over, it became clear that enforcement was not a priority."   Federal probe investigates CFTC staffing    The Government Accountability Office, a congressional watchdog agency, is now investigating the CFTC for its workforce reduction, according to a letter obtained by NPR. This new GAO probe into the CFTC comes after Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., requested a federal investigation into the agency's staffing and fraud enforcement in July.   "It's supposed to be out there regulating the market, but it doesn't appear to be doing it and frankly, doesn't appear to have the people to do it," Warren told NPR in an interview. "I want to know whether or not the watchdog is actually out there doing a little barking, or has the watchdog been locked up somewhere back in the barn?"   The GAO is gathering staff and resources for its investigation into the CFTC and will "initiate" the probe in December.   
   The CFTC did not directly comment on the GAO investigation but did respond to NPR's questions about its staffing levels.   "[The CFTC] is on track to hire roughly 100 employees in mission critical areas by the end of 2026," wrote CFTC spokesman Fulton in a statement. "Like many federal agencies, a number of CFTC staff opted to step away from public service in recent years, and the CFTC will continue to ensure it attracts and retains talented staff dedicated to fulfilling our critical mission."   During 2026, the CFTC has seen a slight uptick in staffing.   While the GAO investigation is narrowly focused on staff reduction, Warren said Congress could use its "power to investigate" possible corruption citing potential Congressional subpoenas and its ability to control the agency's funding.   "But that only happens if Congress has the backbone and right now, led by the Republicans, Congress not only doesn't have a backbone, it doesn't even have any interest in doing it," Warren said.   When asked if a Democratic Congress would subpoena the heads of the CFTC, crypto companies and prediction markets, Warren said, "it is our job to use all those tools to investigate."   Crypto at the White House    In August, the current chair of the CFTC, Michael Selig, celebrated his agency's slowdown in enforcement actions during a White House event featuring the crypto industry.   "The era of political lawfare, debanking and regulation by enforcement is over," Selig said while flanked by crypto CEOs in the Roosevelt Room. "Innovators, like the people in this room, are welcome to the White House — not railroaded to the big house."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Coinbase CEO and co-founder Brian Armstrong speaks as President Donald Trump meets with technology leaders in the Roosevelt Room of the White House, Wednesday, Aug. 19, 2026, in Washington.
                
                    Jacquelyn Martin/Associated Press
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jacquelyn Martin/Associated Press
    

   
   He argued that the U.S. needs to "dominate" these new financial technologies — like crypto and prediction markets — and "write the rules that define the next generation of financial markets." Selig is the sole member of the normally five-member CFTC commission, giving him unchallenged power over the direction of the agency.   
   Before his time at the CFTC, Selig was a corporate lawyer for cryptocurrency firms and prediction markets. His latest financial disclosure report shows that Selig sold between $65,000 and $150,000 in Bitcoin before he became a commissioner.   While Selig wants increased agency rule making for prediction and crypto markets, that requires a massive amount of work and staffing, according to former CFTC director Brian Young, who said the reduction in headcount limits the agency's ability to write new rules.   "With the growth of prediction markets and digital asset trading, the [CFTC] really needs to augment staffing in order to meet these increased responsibilities," Young said. "At the end of the day, they need people to process these applications."   A former CFTC employee — who speaks regularly with current employees — told NPR that the CFTC is so understaffed that it is struggling to execute Trump's 2025 executive order on cryptocurrency.   "My friends that are there are dying," this former staffer told NPR on the condition of anonymity for fear of professional retaliation.   Earlier this year, CFTC Inspector General Christopher Skinner acknowledged the difficulty of short staffing in a recent annual report.   "The CFTC should consider human capital management as a top priority," Skinner wrote. "To ensure the agency has the appropriate talent and skill sets to meet an expanding regulatory landscape."   Meanwhile, the CFTC's work load keeps growing.   In 2025, the agency greenlit six prediction markets — three times the average annual rate over the last decade. This year, the agency has authorized another 6 prediction markets with 18 applications pending.   After the Senate failed to advance a major crypto and banking regulation bill this summer, the CFTC announced this week that it is moving ahead with making its own rules without congressional input.   "The American people deserve clarity, certainty, and consumer protections in the crypto asset markets and the agency is committed to delivering this by incorporating crypto asset transactions into its uniform national market regulatory framework," Selig said in a statement.   
   Still, as of July, the agency's workforce was 16% below its decade-average or 100 staffers short. The CFTC is currently hiring for seven full-time positions.

title: How 'Musk' director Alex Gibney became a critic
description: Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk gestures
body:
Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk gestures on stage at the Capital One Arena after President-elect Donald Trump is sworn in as the 47th President of the United States in Washington, DC on Monday, January 20, 2025.
                
                    Ken Cedeno/UPI/Alamy Live News
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Ken Cedeno/UPI/Alamy Live News
    

   
   Some time ago, Alex Gibney got curious about how Elon Musk accumulated impossibly vast amounts of wealth and power.   So the Oscar-winning documentarian did what he does best, spending four years of deep research into Musk's world to create a film that's nearly as many hours long, each minute kept riveting by a trove of dreadful facts, videos, legal documents and interviews with people close to the tech entrepreneur.   "I started out as — if not an admirer — at least somebody who is sort of interested in what he was doing and liked it," Gibney told Morning Edition host Steve Inskeep.    
   Gibney, who narrates the film, says he was a "proud" owner of a Tesla Powerwall energy storage system at his home and Tesla solar panels on his roof.    But Gibney's perspective shifted as he prepared his film, Musk, which opens in theaters Friday. It's due to stream on HBO in a few months.   "I became increasingly resentful and angry. When [Defense Secretary] Pete Hegseth basically said that they were now going to use xAI to be fully integrated into the Department of War, it was like an out-of-body experience," he said, referring to the artificial intelligence company founded by Musk that's behind the Grok AI assistant.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Alex Gibney spent four years making his nearly four-hour film Musk.
                
                    Jigsaw Productions
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jigsaw Productions
    

   
   Lawsuit threat   The leadup to the film's release has seen some controversy after Musk used several insults to describe Gibney — "an idiot" was among the mildest ones — and threatened a defamation lawsuit over the film.   
   In a letter sent to Gibney's Jigsaw Productions company that emerged in September, Musk attorney Alex Spiro focused on an exchange between Gibney and Ashley St. Clair, a one-time MAGA influencer who had a child with the billionaire.   St. Clair describes in the film text messages Musk sent her before the November 2024 presidential election in which he said he was "feeling more optimistic" about Donald Trump winning because "tomorrow we unleash the anomaly in the matrix."    Musk further told St. Clair that he planned on tapping "'lasers' from space," adding that "I have over 10 thousand lasers in space right now."   
   In the film, Gibney asks St. Clair if she believes Musk's texts referred to satellites owned by his rocket company, SpaceX. She responds, "I don't know where else he has lasers."   NPR has obtained and authenticated the texts between Musk and St. Clair, which were sent on Oct. 6, 2024.     Spiro's letter, which NPR has also reviewed, says that Gibney made a "false" insinuation that SpaceX's Starlink satellites somehow uploaded votes for Trump in swing states, a debunked conspiracy theory.   "We don't claim that he changed votes in the 2024 election. All we do is to show that he was bragging to his lover that he had special access to understanding the outcome of the election in a way that other people didn't," Gibney told NPR. "Was he lying to her or was he just bragging or was he telling us something that we shouldn't know? I don't know. That's for the viewer to decide."   
   Gibney, who's previously investigated the likes of Enron and blood-testing startup executive Elizabeth Holmes in his films, said that when he trained his lens on Musk, he prepared for the possibility that the maverick CEO would try to sue him.   "We had a battery of lawyers reviewing everything that we did. I actually hired an independent fact checker to check our own fact checkers inside. So against the richest man, the truth is not always a defense, but I'm counting on his commitment to the principles of being a free speech absolutist."   Gibney also noted that a lawsuit would also trigger a discovery process by which he could subpoena Musk's internal documents.   Overselling products?   As he took a closer look at SpaceX and Tesla, Gibney noticed that while the two companies "had achieved great things technologically... their stock price was way out of proportion to their actual economic value." The filmmaker says Musk achieved this by overselling his products.   
   SpaceX performed a vital service, ferrying equipment into space… developing rockets that could be reused cheaply.   But the film says Musk cast the company as an even grander venture, forever about to colonize Mars.   Tesla made popular electric cars, but the film says Musk oversold them as self-driving.   According to the film, they weren't made with enough sensors for that, which is why some have crashed. "That's a level of overpromising that leans into fraud," Gibney said.   NPR has reached out to Spiro, Musk's attorney, about the specific claims made in the film but has not heard back.   The broadcast version of this story was produced by Kaity Kline.

title: Carpetbagger allegation, misplaced valor make Nevada's safe red House seat competitive
description: David Flippo, the Republican candidate f
body:
David Flippo, the Republican candidate for Congress in Nevada's 2nd Congressional District, speaks during a primary election night watch party June 9, 2026, in Reno, Nev.
                
                    William Hale Irwin/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        William Hale Irwin/AP
    

   
   RENO, Nev. — The race for Nevada's 2nd Congressional District shouldn't be competitive, just based on history and math. But the Republican Party's nominee, David Flippo, is facing an unusually tough race despite having President Trump's endorsement, bogged down by allegations that he exaggerated his military service and lacks real ties to the district.   "This seat is some kind of competitive like it has never been in the history since it was created," said Mark Amodei, the retiring Republican congressman who has represented the northern Nevada district for the past 15 years. "And you know what I attribute that to? I attribute it to the candidate and the way he's run his campaign."   
   The Washington Post was first to report that Flippo's campaign repeatedly mischaracterized his military service, in fundraising appeals and a video from an earlier congressional run. In the video, the booming voice of a narrator described Flippo as "a recipient of the Bronze Star that he received for Valor."   Candidate blames young staff and grandkids   But Flippo didn't receive a bronze star with the "V" for valor, which requires bravery in battle. It's a big distinction that most veterans notice. Flippo held a press conference where he apologized and blamed a young staffer for mixing up the word "valor" from an award his whole unit received. In an interview with NPR, Flippo said the language about his awards got "edited and convoluted" and he "missed it," then caught it, but somehow it worked its way back into his campaign materials. Still, Flippo said he accepts responsibility.   "Look, part of leadership is taking ownership," he said. "It was just an honest oversight."   Flippo defended wearing the "V" on a ball cap next to his Bronze Star medal. In fact, a photo prominently displayed on his campaign website, showed him wearing two bronze "V" pins. He also wore it regularly at campaign events, including his primary night victory party. This was initially noted by the conservative outlet Nevada News & Views but Flippo addressed the question of why he was displaying those two "V" pins for the first time publicly in his interview with NPR.   
   "You know if you've lived with grandkids, and you know, you kind of know, when you ask them to put those things on your hat," Flippo said before offering further evidence. "Actually, answer me this. I do have another hat that's just like it, because you misplace one or whatever, and that does not have any V devices on it, so and I was like 'where did that other V device go?' So, the grandkids ended up doing that."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                In these screenshots from David Flippo's campaign website, the left shows a photo of his veteran hat featuring two "V" — for Valor — pins next to his Bronze Star pin. On the right is the site after NPR asked why he wears two "V" pins, showing the photo was swapped out.
                
                    Photo Illustration/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Photo Illustration/NPR
    

   
   The campaign removed the photo from his website shortly after our interview. Flippo chalked the controversy up to politics.   "It's just crazy what people are going to go after," he said.   Brand new to the district   Earlier this year, Flippo was running for congress in Las Vegas when Amodei announced he would be retiring. So Flippo swapped districts to run for the open seat, some seven hours to the north by car from where he had been running.    
   With the neon Reno arch behind him and a Trump 47 hat on his head, Flippo announced in a video that he was all in for Nevada's 2nd Congressional District. The district was drawn in 1981 to be strongly Republican and Democrats have never even come close to winning here.   "This is a strong conservative district," Flippo said in an interview with NPR. "I was talking with the people that have endorsed me such as Turning Point and other organizations that are on the conservative side. The belief was that this being a conservative district we should get somebody that is more conservative in this seat."   Flippo handily won the Republican primary with Trump's endorsement. But in recent weeks Republican super PACs have had to come to Flippo's rescue with more than $1 million in TV and digital advertising reservations, according to AdImpact data.   "They must have gotten a poll and had a five alarm fire at headquarters and said we have to pour hundreds of thousands of dollars into that district to save this guy," said Jon Ralston, a longtime Nevada political journalist and founder of the Nevada Independent.   
   Trump won this district by 14 points two years ago, and while Ralston is skeptical a Democrat can ultimately win, he sees signs everywhere that Republicans are treating this like a real race.    
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Teresa Benitez-Thompson (right), the Democratic nominee in Nevada's 2nd Congressional District, attends a candidate open house put on by Moderates for Democracy, in Reno on Sept. 28.
                
                    Tamara Keith/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tamara Keith/NPR
    

   
   Earlier this week, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee added Flippo's opponent Democrat Teresa Benitez-Thompson to its competitive "Red to Blue" program, meaning she'll get extra support from the party committee, which sees this as a winnable race.   "In the state legislature, Teresa was known for crossing the aisle and doing what's right for Northern Nevadans," DCCC Chair Suzan DelBene said in a statement. "Against a scandal-plagued opponent who even Republicans don't like, Teresa is the leader Nevada families deserve."   At a recent candidate meet and greet in southern Reno, Benitez-Thompson played up her deep roots in the district, going back to her early childhood.   "This is home," she said, a not so subtle nod to the fact that her opponent was living and running for office in an entirely different part of the state just six months ago.   A former Miss Nevada, she's now raising four children in Reno. Something she talks about with voters a lot is affordability, including sky-high gas prices and expensive groceries.   "Look, when I talk about the fact that I'm in the middle of this with everyone I really mean it," she tells a voter. "No one has to give me talking points on the cost of groceries. I know exactly what a full grocery cart looks like. I know exactly what prices have been doing in the last year."    
   But there are far more Republican and independent voters in this district than Democrats, a mathematical obstacle for Benitez-Thompson.   "Literally if someone stands still for 5 seconds, I will talk to them," she said in an interview conducted in her kitchen while making her two youngest children an after school snack. "We have focused a lot on reaching outside our Democratic circle."   The candidate meet and greet was attended by voters with a wide range of political affiliations from a conservative-leaning Trump voter who asked Benitez-Thompson about socialism to a Democrat who complained she was too moderate.   
   Grant Sims and his daughter Jessica Sims said they don't always agree politically. He's a former Republican turned independent hoping a blue wave will send a message. She's a Democrat who ticked through a laundry list of concerns about Flippo.   "My brother was in the Marine Corps," Jessica Sims said in explaining her concerns with Flippo's Bronze Star controversy. "Even if he did receive a certain type of medal, but claiming it's more than what he received, I'm not OK with it at all. And I don't like the carpetbagging of him. You know, moving up here because there is a vacancy in the House."   A question hanging over this race, where there hasn't been any recent public polling, is whether these concerns about Flippo have broken through more broadly with voters.   The top issue is affordability   Benitez-Thompson argues that Congress needs to step up and put a check on President Trump and his policies, including the trade wars and his war with Iran, which voters blame for the high prices hitting their family budgets.   Flippo also says affordability is a problem, and admits "the cost of living is not in our favor right now."   
   But he strongly supports the war with Iran and like President Trump sees the elevated prices Americans are experiencing as short term pain, worth it if Iran is prevented from getting a nuclear weapon.   "I feel very confident that once this is taken care of, we'll see gas prices go right back down," he said.   Flippo's military service is a key part of his pitch to voters. In the interview with NPR, he described several tours through the middle east over a 24 year career in the Air Force, including time as a logistics commander, standing up air bases in Iraq.   "My whole career was spent eating the dust and dirt there in the Middle East and that's why I have an understanding of what's going on right now with Iran," he said.   
   Campaign finance records indicate he's loaned $1.6 million to his campaigns this election cycle, a significant share of his reported personal wealth. Flippo said he recently sold his businesses to prepare for serving in congress.   "Yeah, it's a lot, I'm not going to lie. But to me, this country's worth it," he said.   Flippo's campaign did not respond to requests for his financial disclosures, which are overdue.   A spokesman for the National Republican Congressional Committee said Democrats are "delusional" if they think this race is competitive.   But Rep. Mark Amodei disagrees. He said he's heard from a lot of Republicans who are reluctant to vote for Flippo. And he's adamant, he won't be endorsing the man who hopes to be his successor.   "It's like, I'm not hugging this," he said of Flippo. "I'm just not doing it. It's not my last move walking out the door."

schema.headline: Carpetbagger allegation, misplaced valor make Nevada's safe red House seat competitive

title: ICE has quietly used this warehouse as a detention facility all summer, neighbors say
description: A Roxbury, N.J., warehouse was one piece
body:
A Roxbury, N.J., warehouse was one piece of a billion-dollar plan by the Department of Homeland Security to detain migrants.
                
                    José A. Alvarado Jr. for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        José A. Alvarado Jr. for NPR
    

   
   ROXBURY, N.J. — On a warm morning on Sept. 4, masked immigration agents rolled into Dover, N.J.   Footage of the raids rippled across social media, sent people into hiding and reignited rumors that had been circulating for months: Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents were taking people to a nearby warehouse.   
   The warehouse in Roxbury was one piece of a billion-dollar plan by the Department of Homeland Security to detain migrants as part of President Trump's mass deportation efforts.   That plan to convert warehouses into detention centers faced fierce backlash and legal challenges from residents and immigrant advocates. It was largely abandoned, and in several sites, including Roxbury, the government is legally forbidden by a court order from converting them to a detention facility, pending environmental assessments.   But an NPR investigation has found signs that the New Jersey facility is being used. And the state's Office of the Attorney General says it is looking into similar reports.   
   Contractor says he was told Stephen Miller wanted facilities to be "cruel"   In early 2026, Homeland Security bought 11 warehouses to turn into ICE detention facilities. They spent about a billion dollars on these.   NPR spoke to an official at a government contractor whose company was approached to convert several of the warehouses into ICE facilities. He spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation from the government.   "No one that we spoke to at DHS was for this idea whatsoever. The deputy director told us point-blank that they had pushed back very hard on it. Everybody knew warehouses are horrible places to put people," he says.   
   At a meeting with a deputy director at DHS, he says, his company proposed an alternative: FEMA-style camps in Texas that would be more humane.   He says that idea was swiftly shot down. While White House adviser Stephen Miller was not at the meeting, they were told that this was not what Miller wanted.   The contractor says his understanding from that meeting was that "Miller did not want the facilities that were comfortable. He did not want facilities that were humane. We were told point-blank that that was not what the administration wanted."   
   "Steve Miller certainly seemed to make that point to everyone that he wanted it to be cruel. This was what Miller had stated to the DHS at that time, to the DHS director and deputy director. What surprised me was just how adamant the people were that it was going to happen. Damn the consequences. I would say in 25 years of working with the U.S. government, I've never been in that position before."   In a statement to NPR, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said the contractor's comments were "false hearsay allegation(s) from someone who has never even met or talked with Stephen Miller." Bis also said that Miller "has never made any remarks to anyone about wanting illegal aliens to have worse detention facility conditions. It simply isn't true and this is defamatory."   The White House did not respond to repeated requests to speak to Miller directly.   DHS is holding on to the strategically positioned warehouses   Early on, the warehouse plan was met with protests in both conservative and liberal towns. Several state attorneys general filed lawsuits to halt construction, based on environmental concerns.   "It very quickly became an absolute boondoggle," says Michael Wriston, a former military intelligence analyst who co-founded Project SaltBox, a watchdog group that tracks ICE's expansion. "It was really about the optics of people being kept in these cages and these large warehouses. They wanted a lot of what they called B-roll to play on social media, but they didn't do any due diligence of making sure that they conformed with environmental policy or that the construction wouldn't disturb local water tables."   A DHS official who served during Trump's first term, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they feared government retaliation, says that while they were not in the meeting the contractor described to NPR, they had often heard higher-ups in the administration wanting to make a point of showcasing difficult conditions immigrants were being held in.    Then, with the departure of DHS Secretary Kristi Noem in March, there was a shift: Her replacement, Secretary Markwayne Mullin, sought to do less showy immigration crackdowns. Today, Homeland Security is selling several of the warehouses.   
   But they're still holding on to a few, including in Hagerstown, Md., Surprise, Ariz., and Roxbury, N.J. "These locations are very critical to ICE's deportation agenda," says Wriston, "because they fill in the gap in places where ICE does not have a robust detention network. They don't have a lot of jails there." They are also located in areas where there are no partnerships with the police who can house detainees in local jails.   In Maryland, Arizona and New Jersey, following lawsuits from each of the state attorneys general, DHS has either agreed or been ordered by a judge to halt the conversion of the warehouses into detention centers, pending environmental impact assessments. But throughout the summer, in the towns surrounding the Roxbury warehouse, rumors started to bubble.   A summer of arrests and rumors   Over the summer, there was a historic surge in ICE arrests: around 100,000 people in July and August.   In New Jersey, the rumor mill started churning. The Roxbury warehouse is located in a wooded area, on a road right off Route 46. Project NINJA (No ICE in North Jersey Alliance), a coalition that opposes ICE detention expansion, says several neighbors reported vehicles, often in a caravan, speeding up the road.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Dover Council Member Sandra Wittner in Dover, N.J., on Sept. 17.
                
                    José A. Alvarado Jr. for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        José A. Alvarado Jr. for NPR
    

   
   "They're holding people in that warehouse," one woman says in a WhatsApp group in the town of Dover, which is about 15 minutes from Roxbury. "I have a co-worker who was taken there. They hold them there and at night they take them somewhere else." The message was forwarded to NPR by Dover Council Member Sandra Wittner.   "But, you know, it's like third- and fourth-hand accounts," says Wittner. "It just didn't seem probable at the time because of the court order. But it kind of made you scratch your head a little bit."   Then the morning of Sept. 4 happened.   
   "We were taken to the Roxbury warehouse"   A woman says she was driving to work when she saw a raid taking place in Dover. She decided to follow the car carrying people who were detained. "I just needed to know, is he going to Roxbury?"    She took video as she trailed them up Route 46. She asked that NPR not use her name because what happened next made her fearful of what the government might do.   She says the car she was following turned onto the woodsy road that leads to the warehouse.   
   She says she waited to see if there was any more movement.   "And then maybe five minutes after that, a white Dodge Durango started kind of circling around me," she says. "And then on his last loop, he started filming me. He had a yellow case on his cellphone. After that, a black Tahoe started doing the same thing. I was on a public sidewalk, and it was intimidating. It was really intimidating. I'm scared. But I am more scared for our community."   Councilwoman Wittner says she strongly suspects ICE is using the Roxbury warehouse: "The immigration enforcement activity happened in Dover between 7 a.m. and 8 a.m." Wittner points to the woman who was able to follow the vehicle up Route 46: "The last vehicle entered the warehouse road at 8:25 a.m."   Meanwhile, footage of the raid started circulating on social media.   Back in Dover, another woman says she saw the videos as she got her kids ready for school. NPR viewed the videos and confirmed their authenticity.   In one of them, a worker is cornered against a wall by two masked agents. She says she was thunderstruck.   "That's my father," she told NPR.   She asked that we not use her name because she fears being targeted.   At 8:25 a.m., she says, she got a call from her father. He's 59, she says, and he sounded disoriented. He told her he was handcuffed in some kind of jail.   
   She found it strange, she says, because the Roxbury warehouse would be the only place he could have been taken in that short a time span.   She also discovered a friend of hers had been picked up.   
   She hasn't been able to speak to her father since then, and neither has NPR. But NPR located her friend in Honduras, where he's been deported. He requested anonymity, because he fears repercussions for his loved ones who are still in the U.S.   "I was picked up on my way to work, on Friday, Sept. 4. The agents loaded me into a van. They took us to Roxbury," he said.   He says he and the other people detained were handcuffed and held in the parking lot for several hours. He counted nine other men with him. "I just went into a state of shock," he says. "I signed my deportation papers. The next morning I regretted it. But I was scared. Eventually, they transferred us to a real facility."   In a statement to NPR, DHS did not respond to a question about whether it was holding people at the Roxbury location. But it did give NPR a statement it has previously sent about ICE detention, saying DHS upholds strict standards and that immigrants can choose to leave detention by being deported.   "We need our Congress members to conduct an oversight visit yesterday"   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                A member of Project NINJA, a coalition that opposes ICE detention expansion, in Roxbury on Sept. 17.
                
                    José A. Alvarado Jr. for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        José A. Alvarado Jr. for NPR
    

   
   The activists at NINJA say ICE's actions violate the legal order. The order lists several actions ICE can take with the site — mainly upkeep — but nowhere on that list is detention an acceptable action, they say.   Harvard professor Andrew Mergen, a former attorney with the U.S. Department of Justice Environment & Natural Resources Division, says ICE may technically not be violating the court order, which stipulated it would not convert the place into a detention center pending an environmental assessment.   
   Ultimately, Mergen says, the situation shows the limitations of using environmental claims. "The community is acting here to prevent people from being detained," says Mergen. "And the administration seems to have cleverly elided that intention, by sort of saying, 'Well, we're not going to build this facility, but we're going to use this space in furtherance of detention.'"   He says he understands the frustration: "It's just infuriating if what you are trying to do is say 'No. Not here. Not here.' "   
   Wittner says since the raid, she's heard from other close relatives or close friends of two men who were picked up that day, who say they were inside the Roxbury warehouse.   She says the situation is unacceptable: "We need our Congress members to conduct an oversight visit yesterday, quite honestly. We need our state to aggressively pursue this investigation and demand to get inside."   She says DHS has had time "to go in and clean up their mess if they, in fact, got caught doing something that they shouldn't have."   Meanwhile, in Dover, the streets where the raid happened remain deserted.   At an empty diner at lunchtime, a waitress who did not want to be named because of the climate of fear in town says one of the workers who was taken used to come here for a bite.   Then she leans over and asks: "Do you know where they took those men?"   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                The warehouse in Roxbury.
                
                    José A. Alvarado Jr. for NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        José A. Alvarado Jr. for NPR

schema.headline: ICE has quietly used this warehouse as a detention facility all summer, neighbors say

title: Trump approved the military's 1st firing squad execution since WWII. Why now?
description: A memorial to the victims of the Fort Ho
body:
A memorial to the victims of the Fort Hood shooting, pictured in November 2009, outside the apartment complex where Hasan lived.
                
                    Eli Kaplan/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Eli Kaplan/Getty Images
    

   
   President Trump has approved the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, the former U.S. Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people in a shooting rampage at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009.   It would be the first U.S. military execution in over six decades — and the first by firing squad since World War II.   Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell announced the news on X Monday night, writing, "Judgement day for Hasan has finally come." Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in an order released Tuesday that Hasan's execution will take place at Fort Hood on Dec. 3.   
   But Hasan could delay those proceedings if he files a habeas corpus appeal in the federal courts, said Robin Maher, executive director of the nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center.   "The fact that the president has approved Mr. Hasan's death sentence is another step closer to his execution," Maher said. "But that does not mean that his execution will be imminent."   For example, Ronald Gray, who committed multiple rapes and murders near Fort Bragg in the 1980s, is still on military death row despite having had his sentence approved by President George W. Bush in 2008.   It's not clear why the Pentagon is moving forward now, or why it specifically chose a firing squad as the execution method. But some death penalty experts that NPR interviewed suspect it could be connected to Tennessee's botched lethal injection of Christa Pike, which has dominated headlines and reignited debate over the past week.   
   "For years now, states have been pushing this rock of Sisyphus uphill … They're spending millions of dollars, and yet they're having botched executions," said Corinna Lain, whose book, Secrets of the Killing State, was published last year. "So this moment in time is one where states are really thinking about: what are we doing and what best serves the death penalty? Whether the answer to that is firing squad is another question entirely."   The White House referred NPR's questions to the Pentagon, which declined to elaborate beyond Parnell's post.   
   In his announcement, Parnell said Trump had acted on the recommendation of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who said last September that he was "100 percent committed to ensuring the death penalty is carried out for Nidal Hasan."   "This savage terrorist deserves the harshest lawful punishment for his 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood," Hegseth told several media outlets, including The Hill, at the time. "The victims and survivors deserve justice without delays."   
   Hasan was working as an Army psychiatrist in Nov. 2009, when he opened fire at the Fort Hood processing center where troops were preparing to deploy to Afghanistan. He shouted "Allahu akbar" — "God is great" — before killing 13 people and injuring another 32. The attack ended when he was shot by civilian security officers at the scene, leaving him paralyzed from the waist down.   Hasan acted as his own lawyer during his 2013 trial, at which he admitted that "the evidence will clearly show that I am the shooter." The American-born Muslim said he had "switched sides" and turned against the U.S. because of its military actions in the Middle East.   The military jury found Hasan guilty on all counts. He was dismissed from the Army and sentenced to death, which triggered an automatic appeals process that ended only when the Supreme Court denied his final petition in the spring of 2025.   Hasan is one of just four people currently on military death row — all of whom were convicted of murder — according to the Death Penalty Information Center. They are all incarcerated at the United States Disciplinary Barracks at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                This undated photo provided by the Bell County Sheriff's Department shows former Army psychiatrist Maj. Nidal Hasan.
                
                    Uncredited/Bell County Sheriff's Department/Bell County Sheriff's Department
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Uncredited/Bell County Sheriff's Department/Bell County Sheriff's Department
    

   
   The military's last firing squad execution was in 1945    The first recorded execution by shooting on what would become U.S. soil happened in Jamestown, Va., in 1608, when one of the colony's early council members, Capt. George Kendall, was put to death for mutiny. Firing squads have been used relatively sparingly since, including during the Civil War.   
   "On the one hand, it is one of our earliest forms of execution," said Fordham Law School professor Deborah Denno, who has been studying execution methods for 36 years. "On the other hand, it's always been controversial because people associate it with extreme barbarity and … the Wild West."   The U.S. military last executed someone by firing squad in 1945: Private Eddie Slovik was shot for desertion in France, the only U.S. soldier to be executed for that reason since the Civil War.   "They didn't even tell his wife that he had been executed; they just said that he had died in Europe," journalist Charles Glass, who wrote a book about World War II deserters, told NPR in 2013. He said Slovik's case only became public knowledge about a decade later, when an investigative reporter published a book about it in the mid-'50s.   Most of the known U.S. military executions during World War II were done by hanging, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. The last time the U.S. military carried out an execution of any sort was in 1961, when Private John Bennett was hanged for the 1955 rape and attempted murder of an Austrian girl.   "We basically have gone out of the business — until now — of executing people through the military justice system," said Eugene Fidell, who teaches military justice at Yale Law School.   
   The military officially suspended the death penalty after a 1983 court ruling, but reinstated it the following year and specifically designated lethal injection as the standard method. Fidell says that changed with new Army regulations in 2023.   "The regulation was changed to make the choice or the method of execution a matter for the president's discretion," he said. "And obviously, the president has, in this case, approved the use of a firing squad."   Under the current rules, once the president approves an execution, the secretary of the Army decides the time, location and method, to take place within 60 to 150 days.   
   Fidell said he was not surprised by Trump's approval, given his administration's embrace of the death penalty overall and the severity of Hasan's offenses. But he suggested some might find the social media announcement inappropriate.   "The military has lived without executions since 1961, and yet we have here a really serious case," Fidell said. "I think it would have been a lot better had a more formal, dignified means been chosen to disseminate this information."   The Pentagon hasn't held a formal press briefing since May.   The death penalty is already under scrutiny    
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                This photo provided by the South Carolina Department of Corrections shows the state's death chamber in Columbia, S.C., including the electric chair, right, and a firing squad chair, left.
                
                    AP/South Carolina Department of Corrections
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        AP/South Carolina Department of Corrections
    

   
   Denno, who studies the death penalty, doesn't think the timing of the Pentagon's announcement is a coincidence.   
   Denno says Pike's case "is probably the worst that's ever happened." But it's far from the only botched legal injection in recent years, she says, pointing to what she calls a pattern of convicts being "tortured unnecessarily" that has prompted some jurisdictions to seek out alternatives.   The Justice Department made firing squads available for federal executions earlier this year, following a directive from Trump. Seven states now have firing squads on the books as an execution method, which Denno says is the highest number ever recorded.   Denno says firing squads are "the least inhumane method of execution that we have," since, when done properly, death can occur in seconds.   
   But she acknowledges that those have been plagued by issues, too, including last year in South Carolina, when an autopsy revealed that the shooters may have prolonged a prisoner's death by missing his heart.   "There is a humane way to take a life. It's called life without parole," said Lain, the author.   Lain says lethal injections, because of their relative lack of gore, have kept the death penalty "out of sight, out of mind" for many people over the last five decades.   But she sees signs of change. Data analysis by the Death Penalty Information Center shows that death sentences have declined by 90% over the past three decades. Fewer than 50 new ones have been imposed each year since 2015. A 2025 Gallup poll put public support for the death penalty at a five-decade low, with opposition highest among younger generations.   
   "The death penalty in this country is dying its own slow death," she said. She thinks the federal government's embrace of the firing squad, including in Hasan's case, could hasten it even more.

title: Trump proposes Camp David-style presidential retreat at his private Florida golf club
description: FILE - The motorcade for President Donal
body:
FILE - The motorcade for President Donald Trump arrives at Trump International Golf Club, Jan. 2, 2026, in West Palm Beach, Fla.
                
                    Alex Brandon/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Alex Brandon/AP
    

   
   FORT LAUDERDALE, Fla. — President Donald Trump on Wednesday said he wants to develop one of his Florida golf courses into a presidential retreat where his successors can spend quiet weekends on the greens, describing it as "sort of a Camp David " that he says would already have many of the security features needed to host presidents and world leaders.   
   The proposal for the retreat on Trump's private golf course in West Palm Beach would comingle the presidency with Trump's business ventures beyond his time in office, and is the the latest example of Trump seeking ways to leave his imprint on the presidency.   "It's a great idea, and it'll be used a lot," Trump said, claiming it was suggested by the United States Secret Service. "It seems that all presidents play golf."   The plan has already been submitted to local officials. Trump, an avid golfer, rattled off the benefits of the property a short drive from his Mar-a-Lago home during an unrelated event in the Oval Office, noting that it's close to an airport and has some distance from residential homes and tall buildings, which pose security risks.   
   He did not mention that the golf course was the site of an unsuccessful attempt on his life in 2024. Trump was playing at the Trump International Golf Club during a break from the campaign trail when a Secret Service agent spotted an armed man in the trees lining the club's perimeter fence. The man was arrested after a chase and later convicted of trying to kill Trump, and was sentenced to life in prison.   Past presidents have used Camp David, a rustic compound in Maryland, as a weekend retreat and a place to host presidential meetings. Trump has spent less time there, often opting for his own properties, including golf clubs in Florida, New Jersey and Virginia.   Palm Beach County sees what it calls a 'historic opportunity'   Trump's proposal follows other projects by the lifelong real estate developer to build a White House ballroom, gild the Oval Office, erect a triumphal arch, renovate the Kennedy Center, refurbish the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and rebuild a golf course in East Potomac Park. He has also begun planning a future presidential library in a Miami skyscraper.   In a letter to Palm Beach County commissioners last month, first reported by the Palm Beach Post, an attorney who represents the golf course said Trump is offering to designate it as a "U.S. Presidential Golf Course."   
   "Just as Camp David, Windsor Castle, or the Elysée Palace are known worldwide, so too will the Presidential Golf Course in Palm Beach County," Harvey Oyer said in the letter.   
   Palm Beach County Administrator Joseph Abruzzo said in a statement that local officials are eager to explore what this "historic opportunity" could mean to the community. "This likely would further cement Palm Beach County's place on the national and international stage for generations to come," Abruzzo said.   Oyer's letter said the West Palm Beach golf course could be used by current and former presidents, along with visiting foreign heads of state. The Trump Organization owns the golf club but leases the land from the county, which would need to approve any changes.   Under the proposal, the club would pay to build a new presidential lodging and then work with the Secret Service and other agencies to provide free access to the federal government. The retreat would have a separate entrance from the private club, which earned Trump nearly $37 million during his first year back in office, according to his financial disclosure.   "This is a gift that the President would like to share with his successors, the people of America, and his fellow Palm Beach County residents," Oyer wrote. "It should be noted that President Trump will be out of office before this proposed project could be completed so this is a gift to his successors."   
   Oyer highlighted past U.S. presidents who turned over land for public use. Dwight Eisenhower donated his Gettysburg Farm in Pennsylvania to the National Park Service, and Franklin D. Roosevelt donated part of his estate in Hyde Park, New York.   Years before it was bought by Trump, Mar-a-Lago itself was proposed as a "Winter White House."   Businesswoman and socialite Marjorie Merriweather Post left the home to the National Park Service when she died in 1973, but the agency returned the home to her estate in 1980 because of high maintenance costs. Trump bought the property in 1985, and it later became his primary residence.

title: She got Trump's $500 check for health insurance. To her, it's a 'political stunt'
description: Ellen Allen holds the letter from Presid
body:
Ellen Allen holds the letter from President Trump that explains the $500 payment she got. It's about a quarter of what she had to pay monthly in 2026 after her ACA insurance premiums skyrocketed. NPR has redacted her address in the letter to protect her privacy.
                
                    Sue Julian
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Sue Julian
    

   
   Ellen Allen has mixed feelings about the check from the U.S. Treasury and letter from President Trump that arrived at her house near Charleston, W.Va., on Monday.   "I just can't believe it; I mean, that's crazy," says Allen, who's the executive director of a small nonprofit called West Virginians for Affordable Health Care. She says, in her opinion, sending out these checks is a "political stunt."      NPR first spoke to Ellen Allen in the summer of 2025. She was 63 years old at the time and knew she needed coverage from Healthcare.gov even as generous federal subsidies for her premiums were ending. She has a serious eye condition and needs expensive drops to preserve her vision. She advocated for the Republican-controlled Congress to extend the subsidies. It didn't. She ended up using retirement savings to pay $1,967 every month for her premiums from January through August, 2026.   
   Then her birthday came; she turned 65 and was eligible for Medicare. "I was ready at midnight — the first day I could apply, I did," she laughs.   A second check on the way?   Allen chose traditional Medicare, which means she could soon be getting another check from the U.S. Treasury. Last week, President Trump announced that $90 checks will be sent to 20 million people enrolled in Medicare.   "The $90 is — I mean, that's just nothing," Allen says. In her work, she talks to people about healthcare costs all over West Virginia. "People aren't going to be fooled by this," she predicts. "People are hurting. People are feeling the cost of healthcare all year long."   "If they wanted to do something meaningful, they would work on affordable healthcare instead of just sending out checks every now and then," Allen says.   Both checks are directed to select groups. The $500 checks mailed by the Trump administration last week were only sent to people who live in one of the 30 states that use Healthcare.gov for their insurance marketplace. They also make more than $64,000 annually for an individual, which is too much money to qualify for subsidies. These are people, like Allen, who were likely to be hard hit when Congress failed to extend the extra financial help put in place under President Joe Biden.   
   The $90 checks that will be sent to Medicare beneficiaries are only going to certain people enrolled in Medicare Part B. People in Medicare Advantage plans, which are managed by insurance companies, will not get checks.   Can Trump do that?   The checks are hitting people's mailboxes just a few weeks before the midterm elections. The text of a letter sent along with the money touts the Trump administration's efforts on health policy and criticizes the Biden administration.   "This reads like electioneering," says Kathleen Clark, professor of legal and governmental ethics at Washington University law school in St. Louis, Mo. "This reads as though it's intended to influence votes. That is prohibited by law."   Specifically, it would violate the Hatch Act, "the statute that prohibits using federal power and money to influence partisan political elections," she explains. It may also be a use of funds that's unauthorized by Congress.   The money for Healthcare.gov enrollees is from fees insurance companies paid to participate in the marketplace, and the money for Medicare beneficiaries is from a general improvement fund. Neither of these funds has been used for direct payments to enrollees before.   "It looks like a pretty desperate effort to, in essence, bribe the recipients of this letter to vote in gratitude to Trump in the upcoming midterm elections," she adds.   An empowered executive branch   The checks and letters are arriving in people's mailboxes, whether they're legal or not. Clark notes the Supreme Court has given Trump wide latitude many times in the past. "So, of course, he feels empowered to go ahead and do this," she says.   The White House did not respond directly to NPR's questions about electioneering, whether the action is a violation of the Hatch Act or if it is a "political stunt," as Allen put it.   "This is an out-of-touch criticism," Trump administration spokeswoman Allison Schuster wrote in an email. "Americans were overcharged for the operation of the Obamacare exchange, and President Trump returned their hard-earned money. This President will never stop enabling Americans to take control of their health by implementing policies that put money back in their pockets."   
   'Half a tank of gas'   Some Republicans in recent years have advocated for giving more money directly to people rather than to health insurance companies, although the party has yet to settle on a particular approach.   In any case, sending these checks is unrelated to that effort, says Joseph Antos, senior fellow emeritus at the conservative think tank American Enterprise Institute. There's nothing that requires people to use this money for their health.   "From the perspective of the average senior citizen, when they get a $90 check, it's money," he adds, referencing the forthcoming checks for Medicare beneficiaries. "You can go out to McDonald's and buy probably two hamburgers and a shake for $90 [and] maybe buy a half a tank of gas."   A widening trust gap, poll says    A few weeks from the midterm elections, voters say they are struggling with health costs and want candidates to address them, according to a poll released Tuesday by the nonprofit health research organization KFF.   "The cost of healthcare is what's going to be front of mind as they're casting their votes in November," says Ashley Kirzinger, director of survey methodology for KFF. "And what we are seeing is that the Democratic Party has the advantage overall among all voters on which party voters trust to handle healthcare, but they also have the advantage among independent voters, and that's a really important voting bloc for midterm elections."   She says there is "a widening gap" between the Democratic Party and Republicans when it comes to which party voters trust to handle health costs. "It was just a 10-point margin back in April, and now we're seeing it to be a 20-point margin," she says. The poll found 22% of voters trust Republicans on the issue, compared to 42% who trust Democrats.   Where's the credit for GOP candidates?   Antos, of AEI, calls the Trump administration's decision to send out these checks "inexplicable." He describes the move as politically strange, since a Republican administration that disparages Obamacare is investing more money into it, and "unreasonable from a fiscal standpoint," because of the growing national debt.   
   He also notes that most Americans won't be getting these checks. "How about the average, lower-income worker who has employer coverage?" he asks. "They're not getting anything. Why is that? Is that fair?"   He is doubtful the move will have a political benefit for Republican candidates. "For one thing, Trump is not saying that your local congressman did this for you, Trump is saying he did it for you," Antos says. "I don't get it, and I don't see any advantage to anybody, including Donald Trump."   Despite her mixed feelings, Ellen Allen of West Virginians for Affordable Health Care is planning to deposit the $500 check she just received. "I'm not going to send it back," she says. "I'm going to put it in my health savings account and keep working towards healthcare for all."

schema.headline: She got Trump's $500 check for health insurance. To her, it's a 'political stunt'

title: 'Medicare for All' message attracts midterm voters buckling under medical bills
description: Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Abdul
body:
Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Abdul El-Sayed speaks at a news conference in Detroit on Aug. 19, 2026. "Medicare for All!" has become part of the political chants at his rallies.
                
                    Paul Sancya/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Paul Sancya/AP
    

   
   Christina Starks-Clay doesn't know how "Medicare for All" would work exactly, but she's willing to bet it'd be better than what she has now.   
   While standing in line for a Sept. 11 town hall for U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Lansing, she whipped out her phone and pulled up a screenshot.   It was of the $1,000 cashier's check she'd picked up at the bank that day to pay down a chunk of her son's dental bills.   Starks-Clay, an early childhood special education paraprofessional, still owed the dentist $389, even with good dental insurance. Her own cleaning a few weeks before had cost $600.   She tried to talk herself down at the bank, to focus on being grateful for what she could afford.   
   "I'm like, 'Tina, OK, you were in a position for this moment to do this,'" she said. "A lot of people couldn't do what I had to do today. I couldn't do it. But I did it. So I need to hear, how are you going to make this better for everyone?"   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Christina Starks-Clay attended a recent rally for Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. Like many Americans, she likes the idea of "Medicare for All," even if she's unsure how it would work. It sounds like "something that works for everyone. All of us. People work too hard not to have the things that they need," she says.
                
                    Kate Wells/KFF Health News
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Kate Wells/KFF Health News
    

   
   Many who waited in the hot sun that afternoon in a line stretching blocks through downtown Lansing shared similar anxieties.   A man ahead of Starks-Clay talked about watching his brother rack up thousands of dollars in medical debt.   A professor emeritus at nearby Michigan State University worried aloud about his grandkids' medical care, because his adult kids were struggling to meet a $9,000 insurance deductible.   Healthcare workers who'd turned up for the event described patients choosing between affording medication or food, or how they themselves had been financially devastated by a medical crisis.   They all knew El-Sayed's rallying cry by heart, chanting it when the Michigan Democrat took the stage: "Money out of politics! Money in your pocket! Medicare for All!"   Support for Medicare for All is at its highest in at least a decade, according to a new KFF poll. The survey found two-thirds of Americans now favor expanding the government health program that largely covers seniors (about half of whom are enrolled in private plans through Medicare Advantage).   
   But many people don't actually know how to define Medicare for All. Traditionally, the idea has been to establish a single health insurance program, run by the federal government, that would guarantee coverage for Americans and minimize or even eliminate private insurance. How much people like the idea depends on what they're told about it, pollsters have found.   Still, at a time when fewer than half of Americans say they can afford their healthcare, Medicare for All has become a progressive shorthand for radical, systemic change.   "Too many people don't have health insurance, too many people who do have insurance can't afford medical care, and many people are terrified about the costs of being sick," said Jonathan Oberlander, a professor at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill who specializes in the politics of healthcare reform.   "And in an electorate that wants change, that is disenchanted with the status quo, Medicare for All is an important symbol," he said.   That's why Democrats running for Senate seats in the midterm elections in such states as Maine, Minnesota, and Florida tout their support for scrapping the current health insurance system in favor of broad Medicare coverage. But nowhere is the issue as central to a race as in Michigan, where Medicare for All has become synonymous with El-Sayed.   El-Sayed, who trained as a doctor and served as Detroit's top public health official, has campaigned on Medicare for All since his unsuccessful bid for governor in 2018. To Starks-Clay, that means he has a plan and will "stick to it," she said.   That's appealing to voters right now, said Ashley Kirzinger, director of survey methodology at KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News.   "When we ask people what do they want to hear from candidates in regards to healthcare, it's a plan to bring down healthcare costs," Kirzinger said.   
   American Dream or Pipe Dream?   Medicare for All has been the shiny object of progressive politics in previous campaigns, including Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders' 2016 presidential bid and the 2020 Democratic presidential primary. Its popularity rises and falls in cycles, Oberlander said. And today, people are painfully aware their care is getting more expensive and harder to access.   In the first decade or so after the passage of the Affordable Care Act in 2010, the nation's uninsured rate was cut nearly in half. Insurance companies could no longer deny people coverage based on preexisting conditions. Since then, to cover more people, 40 states plus Washington, D.C., have expanded Medicaid, the government health program for those with low incomes or disabilities.   Now it feels as if we're moving backward, Oberlander said. "We are now, in the past two years, in an era where the Trump administration and congressional Republicans have reversed that progress."   Michigan, a battleground state that President Donald Trump won in 2024, saw some of the steepest ACA plan enrollment drops after the GOP-controlled Congress allowed enhanced tax subsidies, which helped people afford their premiums, to expire at the end of last year.   Insurance companies in Michigan hiked individual marketplace rates by an average of 20%.   And up to 355,000 Michiganders are expected to lose their Medicaid coverage in 2028 because of cuts included in Trump's signature law, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, according to estimates from the Urban Institute, a left-leaning think tank.   At El-Sayed's town hall in Lansing, Darleana Ash said patients at the medical diagnostics lab where she works are increasingly skipping tests because they can't afford them.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Republican U.S. Senate candidate Mike Rogers speaks during a Aug. 31 rally in Sterling Heights, Michigan. He opposes Medicare for All, focusing on the trillions of dollars it would cost to put the system in place.
                
                    Nic Antaya/Getty Images
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Nic Antaya/Getty Images

   
   Others drive hours from rural areas because their local labs have closed or are no longer in their insurance networks. She worries about the patients who must choose between their medications and groceries some months.   
   "If you got somebody that's 75, 80 years old, guess what? They're going to go without the medication, because they got to eat," she said.   Packed in near the front of the crowded town hall was Cindy Lou Coolich, a boisterous retiree wearing a campaign T-shirt and cowboy hat.   She spent years working for a company that helped uninsured people enroll in coverage, until she got sick herself. A bout of sepsis nearly killed her and left her disabled.   Suddenly, she was the one enrolling in Medicaid and living on $900 a month from Social Security. She lost the 15-acre horse farm she'd owned, and then everything else, she said. "Except my car."   The saving grace, oddly, was the death of her ex-husband. Because they'd been married for more than 10 years, she could benefit from his Social Security benefits. "So now I'm doing quite well!" she laughed.   But to her, it hardly seemed like the mark of a functioning healthcare system that someone had to die for things to get better.   A universal response   Democrats aren't the only ones responding to voters' healthcare discontent. Republican Mike Rogers, a former Michigan congressman and El-Sayed's opponent, recently released a brief healthcare plan.   "I just can't think of a more important issue to the people of Michigan than healthcare and costs, the rising costs," he said. At a press conference announcing his health platform, he broadly attacked El-Sayed and Medicare for All.   "[If] the government's going to give you something, they have to take it away from someone else," Rogers said.   Under Medicare for All, millions of Michiganders with private health insurance would lose that coverage, he said.   Pointing to estimates that Medicare for All would cost some $4 trillion per year, he said, "Guess what? People pay for that."   (A recent preprint study from Yale researchers found that the cost of implementing Medicare for All, estimated at $4.2 trillion, would save about $1 trillion in healthcare spending.)   
   Rogers' campaign declined an interview request from KFF Health News.   Concerns about increased taxation, disruption to the current system, and reduced access to services can make Medicare for All a political liability in a close election, Oberlander said.   "It doesn't matter if the fears that they're spreading are actually accurate," he said. "Politically, what matters is if they can scare people."   But even if El-Sayed wins in November, the chances of Medicare for All replacing the current system "remain very remote in the short to medium term," Oberlander said.   Given the staunch opposition from Republicans and many moderate Democrats, not to mention the lobbying power of the healthcare industry, massively overhauling the U.S. health system won't suddenly be achievable because of a single Senate candidate.   Thomas "Jermaine" Carey knows this. A self-described activist, he attended a recent El-Sayed town hall in Detroit feeling "kind of sold out" by what he calls the "straight-ticket" Democratic Party.   Medicare for All sounds good, he said. "Do I believe it?" He shrugged.   "It's still America," he said. "You still have super PACs, the lobbyists that control everything."   This story was produced as part of NPR's health reporting collaboration with KFF Health News, a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

schema.headline: 'Medicare for All' message attracts midterm voters buckling under medical bills

title: Toss-ups, triage and targets: How to read the wide-open 2026 House map
